title: If I had…: hypotheses
why: With the conditional (unit 11) and the present subjunctive (unit 15), the learner has everything needed to imagine: this lesson introduces the -ra imperfect subjunctive, built from the indefinido, and the sentence “si tuviera…, viajaría.” It opens the unit “Imagining and regretting,” before the past conditional and the pluperfect.

The imperfect subjunctive: a form born from the indefinido

To imagine a situation that isn't real, English shifts the verb into the past: “if I had time,” “if I were rich.” Spanish does something similar, but with a special tense: the imperfect subjunctive. Si tuviera tiempo… = “If I had time…”. Good news: it's built from a form you already know very well, the indefinido.

The recipe in three steps

  • Take the 3rd person plural of the indefinido: hablaron, comieron, tuvieron.
  • Drop -ron: habla-, comie-, tuvie-.
  • Add -ra, -ras, -ra, -ramos, -rais, -ran.
hablarcomervivirtener
yohablaracomieravivieratuviera
túhablarascomierasvivierastuvieras
él, ella, ustedhablaracomieravivieratuviera
nosotros, nosotrashabláramoscomiéramosviviéramostuviéramos
vosotros, vosotrashablaraiscomieraisvivieraistuvierais
ellos, ellas, ustedeshablarancomieranvivierantuvieran

Two details to remember: the yo form and the él form are identical (si yo tuviera, si él tuviera), and nosotros always has a written accent: habláramos, tuviéramos, fuéramos.

Irregular verbs: no extra effort

Verbs that are irregular in the indefinido keep exactly the same irregularity. If you know tuvieron, you already know tuviera.

InfinitiveIndefinido (ellos)Imperfect subjunctive (yo)
ser / irfueronfuera
tenertuvierontuviera
estarestuvieronestuviera
poderpudieronpudiera
hacerhicieronhiciera
decirdijerondijera
quererquisieronquisiera
sabersupieronsupiera
venirvinieronviniera
ponerpusieronpusiera
dardierondiera
leerleyeronleyera
dormirdurmierondurmiera
pedirpidieronpidiera

For hay, just learn the form hubiera: si hubiera = “if there were.” As in the indefinido, ser and ir share the same form: si fuera más joven (if I were younger), si fuera a Sevilla (if I went to Seville). Context tells them apart.

You'll also come across a second form in -se: hablase, tuviese, fuese. It means exactly the same thing and is mostly seen in writing. You just need to recognize it: in your own sentences, use the -ra form.

", "

Si tuviera tiempo, viajaría más

The hypothetical sentence works just like English: after si, the imperfect subjunctive (where English uses the past: “if I had”), and in the other half, the conditional (English “would”), which you saw in unit 11.

EnglishSpanish
If I had time, I'd travel more.Si tuviera tiempo, viajaría más.
If I were rich, I'd buy a house.Si fuera rico, compraría una casa.
If the weather were nice, we'd eat outside.Si hiciera buen tiempo, comeríamos fuera.
What would you do if you won the lottery?¿Qué harías si ganaras la lotería?

As in English, the order can be reversed: Viajaría más si tuviera tiempo. And the negative doesn't change anything: Si no lloviera, saldríamos.

Trap #1: never the conditional after si

In English, “if I would have time” is wrong. Same in Spanish: never say “si tendría.” And no present subjunctive either: “si tenga” doesn't exist. After hypothetical si, there's only one option: the imperfect subjunctive.

Si tuviera dinero, me compraría un coche nuevo.If I had money, I'd buy myself a new car.

Real or imaginary?

It all depends on how likely the situation is. If it's possible, keep the structure you know: si + present, then future or command. If it's unlikely or impossible, switch to the imperfect subjunctive. English works the same way (“if I have time, I'll go” / “if I had time, I'd go”).

SituationStructureExample
possiblesi + present → futureSi tengo tiempo, iré al gimnasio.
possible, advicesi + present → commandSi tienes tiempo, llámame.
imaginary, unlikelysi + imperfect subjunctive → conditionalSi tuviera tiempo, iría al gimnasio.

To give advice, you know yo que tú (unit 11). Here's its long version, very common, and just like English: Si yo fuera tú, aceptaría el trabajo. (If I were you, I'd take the job.)

", "

Ojalá…: dreaming out loud

You know ojalá + present subjunctive for a possible wish: Ojalá haga sol mañana (I hope it's sunny tomorrow). With the imperfect subjunctive, ojalá expresses an unlikely or even impossible wish, like English “I wish…” or “if only…”, which also shift to the past.

WishSpanishEnglish
possibleOjalá apruebe el examen.I hope I pass the exam.
unlikelyOjalá tuviera más vacaciones.I wish I had more vacation!
impossibleOjalá estuvieras aquí.I wish you were here!

The choice depends on what you think: Ojalá venga Pablo (he might come), Ojalá viniera Pablo (I'd love that, but I don't really believe it).

Traps for English speakers

  • After hypothetical si: imperfect subjunctive, never the conditional or present subjunctive.
  • The nosotros accent: si fuéramos, si pudiéramos, si habláramos.
  • Fuera comes from both ser and ir: si yo fuera tú (to be), si fuera a Madrid (to go).
  • Hay becomes hubiera: Si hubiera menos tráfico, iría en bici.
Si viviera en Madrid, iría al Retiro todos los domingos.If I lived in Madrid, I'd go to the Retiro every Sunday.
¡Ojalá pudiéramos quedarnos una semana más!I wish we could stay one more week!
